interview_metadata.name: Tyler Brizendine
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Waco, Texas, in 1956, and grew up in a pretty ordinary middle-class Anglo family in Central Texas. My folks believed in manners, steady work, and not making a spectacle of yourself, but they also let me be curious. By the time I was a teenager in Austin, the city was changing fast, with music, students, politics, and art all mixed together, and that opened my head up some. I went to college for a while at the University of Texas but did not finish a degree; I needed work and I had a knack for staying calm on the telephone. I started in telephone operations when switchboards and paper logs were still part of the job, then moved through call centers, customer service desks, PBX systems, and later VoIP. I married in my late twenties, had one daughter, and later divorced after years of trying to make two different temperaments fit. These days I live by myself in Austin, do part-time consulting and training, volunteer with seniors on smartphone skills, hike, cook Tex-Mex, and spend a lot of time around the Blanton and local music rooms.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood, what scene comes back first?
follow_ups.response: Sitting at the kitchen table while my mother balanced coupons and my father read the paper after work. There was always iced tea, usually beans or chicken on the stove, and a sense that tomorrow you got up and did your part.

follow_ups.question: What drew you toward telephone work instead of another line of work?
follow_ups.response: I had a good ear for tone. I could tell when somebody was scared, angry, confused, or just lonely, and I learned that a calm voice and accurate notes could solve a surprising number of problems.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The big crossroads was leaving college without finishing. I was taking classes, working odd hours, and telling myself I would get organized next semester, but money was tight and I was not focused enough. A supervisor at a telephone answering service offered me a full-time position because I showed up on time and handled difficult callers without snapping. I remember thinking I could either keep drifting through school or commit to a skill and become dependable. I took the job, and it became a whole career. I sometimes wonder what a degree would have done for me, but that choice gave me stability and a craft.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to before making that choice?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mother and one older coworker named Don. My mother worried about me quitting school, but Don told me, 'If you take it seriously, nobody can replace good judgment on the phone.'

follow_ups.question: What changed immediately after you chose the job?
follow_ups.response: My days got structured. I had a regular shift, a notebook for procedures, and rent money that was not theoretical.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, though not a dramatic one. I sat with the offer letter, looked at my bills, and decided I needed to build from where I actually was.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel like giving something up?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it felt like giving up the version of myself who finished college on schedule.

follow_ups.question: Did you regret it later?
follow_ups.response: A little, but not bitterly. I kept learning through work, books, museums, and people.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Better advising probably would have helped. I did not know how to navigate aid, scheduling, or part-time degree options, and I was too proud to ask many questions.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A practical counselor who could say, 'Here are two classes, here is your work schedule, here is a path.'

follow_ups.question: Did your employer help you grow after that?
follow_ups.response: Yes, informally. Good supervisors taught me call handling, documentation, and how to train new people.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am divorced and not living with a partner. I have one daughter, Emily, who lives in Round Rock with her husband and my grandson. We are close, but not the kind of close where we talk five times a day. We usually have Sunday lunch twice a month, and I try to show up for school programs or soccer games when my knees and schedule allow. My younger sister Janet lives in Georgetown, and she is the person who knows the old family stories best. My parents are both gone, and that still catches me sometimes, especially when I am doing genealogy research and want to ask one more question.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your daughter usually do together?
follow_ups.response: We often meet for lunch at a casual Tex-Mex place or I bring enchiladas over. She teases me for making the salsa too hot.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your sister?
follow_ups.response: About once a month in person, more often by phone. We trade family records and check on each other's health appointments.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My former wife, Linda, is still part of the wider family because of our daughter. We are polite and practical now, which took some years to arrive at.

follow_ups.question: Do you communicate directly with her?
follow_ups.response: Only when there is a family event or something involving Emily.

follow_ups.question: Is the relationship tense?
follow_ups.response: Not anymore. It is limited, but civil.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are mostly from three circles: the Saturday walking group, the arts crowd, and a few former coworkers. I have coffee most Wednesdays with a retired dispatcher named Miguel, and we talk about technology, baseball, and whatever city council has stirred up. There is also Nora, who helps me organize the monthly community art talks; she has a better eye for promotion than I do. I date occasionally, but I am not in a serious relationship.

follow_ups.question: Who do you spend the most regular time with?
follow_ups.response: Miguel and the walking group. That Saturday morning rhythm keeps me socially honest.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually meet friends?
follow_ups.response: Coffee shops near Hyde Park, the Blanton, community center courts, or small music venues.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in the 78705 area, near the university side of Austin, in a modest one-bedroom apartment. It is an interesting mix of students, older renters, small apartment buildings, buses, bicycles, coffee shops, and noise at odd hours. I like being close to museums, lectures, and bus routes because I do not want to drive everywhere. The downside is that rents keep climbing and the neighborhood can feel temporary because students cycle in and out. Still, I can walk to errands, catch music without making it a whole expedition, and stay connected to the city.

follow_ups.question: What is a usual errand route for you?
follow_ups.response: I walk to the pharmacy, stop for coffee, and sometimes take the bus toward the Blanton or Central Market.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by first name. Mostly we exchange mail mix-ups and hallway greetings.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe, especially in the daytime. At night I pay attention, avoid a couple of poorly lit blocks, and do not leave anything visible in my car.

follow_ups.question: Have you had any direct safety problems?
follow_ups.response: Only a car break-in years ago, nothing violent.

follow_ups.question: What makes you feel safer?
follow_ups.response: Foot traffic, lighting, and knowing the bus stops and open businesses.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is access: art, music, medical care, buses, and people from many backgrounds. The downside is cost, traffic, and sometimes feeling like Austin is trying to become too polished for ordinary people.

follow_ups.question: What change bothers you most?
follow_ups.response: Older places disappearing for expensive apartments.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: The cultural life and the fact that my routines are built around this area.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live alone. It is just me in a one-bedroom apartment, with too many books, a small kitchen, and a balcony where I keep cilantro, mint, and a struggling basil plant. My daughter and grandson visit sometimes, but nobody stays long-term. Living alone suits me because I like quiet mornings and organized spaces.

follow_ups.question: How do you use the space day to day?
follow_ups.response: The dining table doubles as my consulting desk and genealogy sorting station.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever feel lonely living alone?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes in the evenings, but I manage it by keeping regular social commitments.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. I am the only permanent household member.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone receive mail there?
follow_ups.response: No, only me.

follow_ups.question: Any regular overnight guest?
follow_ups.response: No, not regularly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My grandson has stayed overnight once or twice, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: When was the last time?
follow_ups.response: Last summer, when my daughter and son-in-law had an early appointment.

follow_ups.question: Where does he sleep?
follow_ups.response: On a foldout cot in the living room.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: Correct, no one.

follow_ups.question: Any pets away or boarded?
follow_ups.response: No pets.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Mondays and Wednesdays I usually do consulting calls or training prep from about 9 in the morning until early afternoon. Tuesdays I volunteer at the senior center helping people with smartphones, passwords, photos, and video calls. Thursdays are often errands, laundry, and reading, and Friday evenings I may go hear jazz or folk music if the ticket is reasonable. Saturday morning is my walking group, usually around Lady Bird Lake or a Hill Country trail if someone is driving. Sundays are quieter: groceries, cooking, maybe lunch with my daughter twice a month, and a Rangers game on the radio or TV.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up?
follow_ups.response: Around 6:30. I make coffee, check the weather, and write down the day's appointments.

follow_ups.question: What is your most fixed weekly commitment?
follow_ups.response: Saturday walking group. I miss it only for illness, travel, or serious weather.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am semi-retired from full-time telephone operations, but I still work part-time as a call-center and phone-systems consultant. I train small businesses on call flow, scripts, logs, PBX basics, and VoIP etiquette. A typical week is 18 to 24 paid hours, mostly mornings and early afternoons, with occasional evening training if a client needs it after business hours. I also mentor a few younger customer service employees from my old network, though not all of that is paid. I like work that has a start time, a checklist, and a clear result.

follow_ups.question: Where do you do the consulting?
follow_ups.response: Mostly from home over video or phone, sometimes at a small office or business site in Austin.

follow_ups.question: What do clients usually need most?
follow_ups.response: They need scripts that sound human and procedures that keep calls from falling through cracks.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep a pretty disciplined budget every Sunday evening. I also tend my balcony herbs, plan meals, and keep a medication and appointment list even though I am not on anything complicated. Once a month I help host a community art talk, which means confirming the artist, arranging chairs, checking the microphone, and making sure nobody talks over the guest. I attend a genealogy group monthly and usually bring one folder of family documents to sort.

follow_ups.question: What tools do you use to stay organized?
follow_ups.response: A paper planner, a spreadsheet for money, and phone reminders for appointments.

follow_ups.question: How much time does the art talk take?
follow_ups.response: Maybe six hours a month counting planning, setup, the event, and follow-up emails.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is that I cut back from more regular contract hours to a smaller consulting load. I wanted more time for health, art events, and my grandson, and frankly I do not recover from packed weeks like I did at 45. I also added pickleball on some Tuesday afternoons because my doctor said I needed more balance and lateral movement. I am trying to keep screens out of the last hour before bed, with mixed success.

follow_ups.question: When did you reduce your work hours?
follow_ups.response: Late last year, around November.

follow_ups.question: Has the change helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I am less irritable and my knees feel better when I pace the week.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My daughter is grown, so I do not have school-age children at home. My grandson is in elementary school, and from what Emily tells me, mornings are breakfast, backpack, and a quick drive to school. After school he has soccer once or twice a week and sometimes a robotics club. My role is mostly granddad support: I show up for a game, bring snacks, or cover an afternoon if Emily is in a bind.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help with your grandson?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month, more during school breaks.

follow_ups.question: What do you two do together?
follow_ups.response: We build simple kits, watch baseball highlights, or make tacos.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My direct experiences have been limited. I have had traffic stops, one car break-in report, and a couple of calls when I worked phone lines where police had to be dispatched. As a white older man, I know I have generally been treated with patience. That is part of why I listen carefully when friends and neighbors describe very different experiences.

follow_ups.question: What happened during your most recent traffic stop?
follow_ups.response: I was pulled over for a brake light. The officer was professional, gave me a warning, and I fixed it the next day.

follow_ups.question: Did call-center work affect how you think about police?
follow_ups.response: Yes. You hear how quickly a routine situation can become frightening for people.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Reporting my car break-in stands out because it was handled politely but nothing really came of it. I understood they had bigger matters, but it made me see how limited the system can be.

follow_ups.question: What was stolen?
follow_ups.response: An old GPS unit, sunglasses, and some change.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your behavior?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became strict about leaving the car empty.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I had one cousin who had a DWI years ago, and it caused a lot of family embarrassment and some real financial trouble for him.

follow_ups.question: Were you close to that cousin?
follow_ups.response: Not especially, but close enough to hear the family fallout.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you think about drinking and driving?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I use rideshare or skip drinking if I am driving.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in almost every election, including local ones. I missed a runoff once years ago and felt foolish because local races are where daily life gets shaped. I usually vote early at a nearby location, and I read the League of Women Voters guide before I go. I am not a yard-sign-every-season person, but voting is a basic responsibility to me.

follow_ups.question: Which elections do you pay most attention to?
follow_ups.response: City council, school board, state races, and presidential elections.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss voting with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with my daughter, though we do not always agree on priorities.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself a moderate Democrat with old Texas habits of fiscal caution. I believe government has a role in health care, infrastructure, education, and protecting civil rights, but I also want programs administered competently. Austin made me more open-minded over the years on race, immigration, LGBTQ issues, and environmental questions. At the same time, I still hear my father's voice about waste and debt, so I read budgets more than slogans. I do not like cruelty dressed up as toughness. I also do not like politics that treats every person on the other side as stupid. My general view is that a decent society should be practical, fair, and honest about who has been left out.

follow_ups.question: What issues matter most to you locally?
follow_ups.response: Housing affordability, public transit, homelessness, water, and preserving cultural spaces.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel most conflicted?
follow_ups.response: Growth. Austin needs housing, but I hate seeing older neighborhoods and venues erased.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on housing and health care than I used to be. When you are older and watching rent, insurance, and medication prices, those stop being abstract. I have also become less patient with conspiracy thinking because I saw how misinformation confused seniors during COVID and vaccine rollout. On the other hand, I try harder now to ask why people distrust institutions instead of just dismissing them.

follow_ups.question: What changed your thinking on misinformation?
follow_ups.response: Helping seniors with phones and seeing alarming posts forwarded as fact.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed parties?
follow_ups.response: No, but I have become more firmly Democratic than I was in younger years.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me somewhat to a lot, especially after hearing younger coworkers and artists talk about experiences I had never had to navigate. I did not grow up using the language people use now, but I understand enough to know that unequal treatment is real. The protests made me read more and listen more carefully. I would not claim to be an expert or activist, but I was moved by it.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend any protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one daytime gathering in Austin, masked and toward the edge.

follow_ups.question: What did you read?
follow_ups.response: Articles on policing history, some essays by Black writers, and museum materials on racial representation.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about accountability, unequal risk, and who gets the benefit of the doubt. In telephone work, I learned that tone and assumptions shape outcomes before facts are even gathered. That seems true in policing too, but with much higher stakes. I support better training, transparency, and consequences for misconduct, and I also think communities need services that are not police for every social problem.

follow_ups.question: Do friends agree with you?
follow_ups.response: Most Austin friends do, though some older relatives think the movement went too far.

follow_ups.question: What feels hardest to resolve?
follow_ups.response: Balancing public safety with real accountability and trust.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country is still carrying history in ways some white people would rather not see. Genealogy taught me that families inherit more than names; they inherit property patterns, opportunities, silences, and stories. Being in Austin, I see both diversity and segregation by cost and neighborhood. I try to be humble about what I know and direct about what I can support, like fair schools, voting access, and honest history.

follow_ups.question: Has genealogy affected this view?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Looking at records makes history less abstract and less flattering sometimes.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with your grandson?
follow_ups.response: Only age-appropriate things, like fairness and listening to people's experiences.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and family, attended one local gathering, donated a modest amount to a bail and legal aid fund, and included more diverse artists in our community art talks.

follow_ups.question: Were those conversations difficult?
follow_ups.response: Some were. I try to keep my voice level and ask questions instead of escalating.

follow_ups.question: Was the art programming intentional?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Public conversation should not only feature people who look like me.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My daughter is more openly progressive than I am and talks about these issues directly with her friends. My sister is sympathetic but cautious, and she worries about disorder more than I do. My walking group is mixed; some people joined marches, others mostly read and talked. A few older acquaintances got defensive, especially online, and I stepped back from some conversations because they were not productive.

follow_ups.question: Did any relationship change because of it?
follow_ups.response: A couple of Facebook connections cooled off, but no close family break.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced you most?
follow_ups.response: Younger coworkers and artists who spoke plainly about daily experiences.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For 69, I would say I am in decent but not heroic health. I have mild high blood pressure controlled with medication, some knee arthritis, and I watch my cholesterol. Walking and hiking help, and pickleball is teaching me that my balance is not what it used to be. I sleep fairly well if I keep coffee to the morning. My doctor would like me ten pounds lighter, and she is probably right.

follow_ups.question: What medications do you take?
follow_ups.response: A blood pressure medication and a statin, both generic.

follow_ups.question: What limits you physically?
follow_ups.response: Steep descents on hikes and too much standing on concrete.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I keep routines: Saturday walks, simple breakfasts, and cooking at home. It is hard because Tex-Mex food is not always gentle on salt, cheese, or portion size, especially the way I like it. Heat in the summer also makes outdoor exercise tricky. Having friends who walk helps more than any lecture.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit is most reliable?
follow_ups.response: Walking early before the heat gets serious.

follow_ups.question: What habit slips first?
follow_ups.response: Late-night snacking during baseball games.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing dramatic like cancer or a broken bone. The main thing was a knee flare-up after a rocky hike near Enchanted Rock last year. I had swelling for a couple of weeks, did physical therapy, and learned I needed better shoes and trekking poles. My blood pressure also crept up, so the doctor adjusted my dose. It was a reminder that maintenance is not optional anymore.

follow_ups.question: Are you still doing physical therapy exercises?
follow_ups.response: Yes, three or four mornings a week when I behave myself.

follow_ups.question: Did it change where you hike?
follow_ups.response: I choose flatter trails more often and avoid showing off.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health does not prevent me from working, but it affects how much I schedule. I avoid back-to-back full days because stress, sitting, and knee stiffness pile up.

follow_ups.question: Have you turned down work for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a few on-site trainings that required long standing days.

follow_ups.question: Does health affect family care?
follow_ups.response: Only in that I cannot chase my grandson like a younger granddad.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My sister had a breast cancer scare that turned out not to be cancer, but those weeks were tense. My daughter also had a rough time with postpartum anxiety years ago, and I learned to take emotional health more seriously. I helped drive my parents to appointments before they passed, so medical caregiving is familiar territory. These days nobody immediate is in crisis, thankfully.

follow_ups.question: Who do you usually help with appointments?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my sister if she needs a ride or second set of ears.

follow_ups.question: How do you support your daughter now?
follow_ups.response: I offer practical help and try not to give advice unless asked.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have Medicare now with a supplemental plan, so I am better positioned than many people. Before Medicare, premiums and deductibles were a real worry, and I delayed dental work more than once. Getting appointments can still be slow, especially specialists. I have not skipped essential care recently, but I compare costs and ask whether tests are truly necessary.

follow_ups.question: What care did you delay?
follow_ups.response: A crown and some dental repair work because the price was steep.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a primary care doctor in Austin I see twice a year.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing I would call formal alternative medicine. I use stretching, heat, ice, turmeric tea occasionally, and the old family habit of honey and lemon when your throat is scratchy. My daughter tried acupuncture once for back pain and said it helped a little. I am open to complementary things, but I still want evidence and I do not skip regular medicine.

follow_ups.question: Do you take supplements?
follow_ups.response: A basic vitamin D supplement because my doctor recommended it.

follow_ups.question: Any herbal remedies from childhood?
follow_ups.response: Mostly home kitchen remedies, not a formal tradition.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke and never had more than a brief young-man phase with cigarettes. I drink beer, usually craft cerveza with dinner or during a game, but I keep it modest. In a normal week it might be two or three beers total. During hard times I am more likely to cook, walk, or clean the apartment than drink heavily.

follow_ups.question: What kind of beer do you like?
follow_ups.response: Local lagers or Mexican-style beers, not the heavy high-alcohol stuff.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever worried about drinking?
follow_ups.response: No, but I watch it because of blood pressure and family examples.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I use prescriptions as directed, not for coping. For pain, I take over-the-counter ibuprofen occasionally, usually after a long hike or pickleball. I do not use marijuana; I tried it a couple of times decades ago and did not enjoy feeling foggy. The most recent pain medicine was two ibuprofen after my knee got sore from a community center pickleball game.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about pain medication?
follow_ups.response: A little, so I avoid taking it daily and ask the doctor when needed.

follow_ups.question: Any sleep aids?
follow_ups.response: No regular sleep aids. I use reading and routine.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Medicare, a supplemental plan, and careful budgeting. My prescriptions are generic, which helps. Dental is the weak spot because coverage is thin and costs jump quickly. My daughter has insurance through work, and my sister has Medicare too. We compare notes on doctors and costs like many older folks do.

follow_ups.question: Is health care a monthly budget line?
follow_ups.response: Yes, premiums, prescriptions, copays, and a little set aside for dental.

follow_ups.question: Who helps with decisions?
follow_ups.response: I decide for myself, but my daughter reviews big paperwork if needed.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccine. I got my COVID shots and boosters, flu shots most years, and the shingles vaccine after seeing a friend suffer through shingles.

follow_ups.question: Did you have side effects?
follow_ups.response: A sore arm and fatigue for a day, nothing serious.

follow_ups.question: Do you encourage others?
follow_ups.response: Gently, especially seniors I tutor, but I do not badger them.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary doctor is first. I also look at CDC information, the local public health department, and sometimes major medical centers like Mayo Clinic. I do not trust random forwarded posts or videos with dramatic music. When seniors ask me about phone links, I help them check whether the source is real before they act on it.

follow_ups.question: Do you watch TV news for medical information?
follow_ups.response: Only lightly. I prefer written sources I can compare.

follow_ups.question: Who in your family asks about vaccines?

follow_ups.response: A short drive away.

follow_ups.question: Did you visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: A few times, usually after school or during events.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked steadily.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when we were younger.

follow_ups.question: Did he change jobs often?
follow_ups.response: No, he valued steady employment.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He worked as a parts manager for an auto supply business. He tracked inventory, dealt with mechanics and customers, ordered parts, and made sure the right item got to the right person. He was methodical and expected accuracy.

follow_ups.question: Did his work influence you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially the importance of records and reliability.

follow_ups.question: Was he handy?
follow_ups.response: Very handy, though not always patient teaching it.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: It was an auto parts supplier serving repair shops and individual customers. They did not manufacture parts; they stocked, sold, ordered, and delivered them. It was a practical place where mistakes cost time and trust.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever work there?
follow_ups.response: Only small errands, not as a real job.

follow_ups.question: What did you notice about that workplace?
follow_ups.response: The countermen knew customers by voice and by vehicle.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope I am still independent, still walking, still useful, and still curious. I would like to keep consulting part-time but be more selective, maybe only training and mentoring instead of troubleshooting emergencies. I hope the community art talks become a steady little institution where local artists feel respected and regular people feel welcome asking questions. I want to take that Mexico City mural trip if the budget and health line up. I also want to be present for my grandson as he gets older, not as a bossy elder but as someone dependable. Mostly I hope my life stays modest, connected, and not ruled by fear.

follow_ups.question: What would independence mean day to day?
follow_ups.response: Managing my home, transportation, money, and appointments without burdening my daughter.

follow_ups.question: What would make the next few years feel successful?
follow_ups.response: Good health, meaningful work, a few memorable trips, and strong family ties.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value steadiness, kindness, curiosity, and keeping your word. Family matters deeply, but I also value the wider circle: neighbors, artists, coworkers, seniors learning a phone, the walking group waiting at 8 a.m. I believe a life should be useful without becoming joyless. Good conversation, honest work, music in a small room, a trail in the morning, and a meal shared at the table are about as close as I get to a creed.

follow_ups.question: Which value did your parents teach most strongly?
follow_ups.response: Reliability. If you said you would do something, you did it.

follow_ups.question: Which value did Austin teach you?
follow_ups.response: Curiosity about people who live differently than I do.
